analysis.one_liner: Lets consumer product safety regulators write safety standards for firearms.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced in February 2026 and referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee, where it has had no further action and no vote.
analysis.plain_summary: Under current law, the Consumer Product Safety Commission — the agency that sets safety rules for things like cribs and space heaters — is barred from regulating firearms, gun parts, and ammunition. This bill deletes that exclusion, letting the agency issue safety standards for guns. The bill went nowhere after its referral: it was sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee on the day it was introduced and has not been scheduled for any hearing or vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers and households exposed to gun injuries would benefit if the safety agency can require design features and other safety measures on firearms sold to the public. The agency itself gains authority it has been explicitly denied since 1976.

how_it_helps.text: The bill amends the Consumer Product Safety Act to strike the subparagraph that excludes pistols, revolvers, and other firearms from the definition of 'consumer product', which is what currently blocks the CPSC from issuing safety standards for them [S3].
The CRS summary states the bill allows the CPSC to issue safety standards for firearms and firearm components, which under current law are excluded from the agency's rulemaking authority [S2].

Safety standards for consumer products are how the federal government requires things like child-resistant packaging and non-tip furniture; applying the same authority to firearms would let the agency address design-related injury risks rather than leaving gun design wholly unregulated [S2].

analysis.who_pays: Firearm and ammunition manufacturers would bear the cost of complying with any safety standards the agency issues, and gun-rights advocates argue the authority could be used to impose requirements that make guns costlier or impractical to sell.

drawbacks.text: The bill only permits the agency to write standards; it does not itself set any rule, so its real-world effect depends entirely on what the CPSC later does, and standards aimed at product design would not address who can obtain a gun — the question most gun-violence policy fights over [S2].

The strongest good-faith objection is that a consumer-safety framework could be used to impose design requirements that effectively burden lawful firearm ownership, which is why Congress wrote the exclusion into the Consumer Product Safety Act in the first place; the bill's text addresses this concern only by leaving the CPSC's ordinary rulemaking procedures in place [S3].
Manufacturers would absorb compliance costs from any future standards, costs that could be passed on to buyers [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill is a narrow, permissive change: it reopens a door closed by statute in 1976 but writes no rules itself, so its benefits are contingent on later agency action while its costs — compliance burdens on manufacturers and possible price pass-through — are also contingent. The honest case for it is that firearms are the only consumer product Congress has categorically barred the safety agency from touching; the honest case against is that the authority could be stretched beyond mechanical safety into de facto restrictions on ownership.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee the day it was introduced and has sat there since, with no hearing or vote scheduled.

narrative.text: Representative Robin Kelly of Illinois introduced the Firearm Safety Act of 2025 on February 11, 2026 [S1].
The same day, the bill was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce, which is the only action in its history [S5].
Thirty-three House Democrats cosponsored the bill; no Republicans did [S4].
The committee has taken no further steps — no markup, hearing, or vote appears in the action history [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Firearm manufacturers remain exempt from consumer product safety regulation, which is the status quo the bill would have ended. Consumers are no better or worse off than before, since no safety standard was ever proposed.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Firearm makers keep their regulatory exemption

for.name: Robin Kelly
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to let the CPSC set firearm safety standards.

sides.party_line_note: All 34 sponsors and cosponsors are Democrats; no Republican has signed on, and the bill sits in a committee controlled by the Republican majority.

industries.note: The bill ends their categorical exemption from the Consumer Product Safety Act, exposing them to safety standards and compliance costs for the first time since 1976. Consumers' interest in design-safety rules runs directly against the industry's interest in remaining unregulated. [S2, S3] — sources cited in entry text: S2, S3.

Retailers would have to stock only products meeting any future standards and could face new labeling or handling requirements, but they would face no direct regulation themselves until the CPSC acts. The industry's overall interest in keeping the exemption intact runs against consumers' interest in safer products.

analysis.trajectory: The bill has the typical profile of one that dies in committee: it was introduced late in the second session, referred to a committee controlled by the opposing party, has no Republican cosponsors, and no hearing or markup has been scheduled. Barring an unusual push, it will expire at the end of this Congress without a vote.
